title: Weighing
summary: Most rounds end with both sides winning something. Weighing tells the judge why your impacts matter more, using magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility.

p: By the last speeches, each side usually has an argument or two still standing. If you only say "we win our argument," the judge has to decide on their own which argument matters more, and they may not choose yours. **Weighing** is comparing impacts out loud so the judge doesn't have to guess.
Weigh *comparatively*: not "our impact is big," but "our impact is bigger than theirs, because...".

rows: How big is it? How many people, how much harm or good?
"Their impact affects one district's budget; ours affects every student's health."
How likely is it to happen?
"Their harm needs four things to go wrong in a row; ours is already happening."
"Students lose sleep starting the first week; their cost shows up years from now, if ever."
"A bad budget year can be fixed next year. A lost species can't be brought back."
table.note: Others you'll hear: **scope** (how widely it spreads), **severity** (how bad for each person), **strength of link** (how sure the cause is), and **values** (which matters more, like liberty or safety).

p: Often one side has a huge but unlikely impact, and the other a smaller but near-certain one. Neither measure wins automatically. Make the case for *your* measure: "A one-in-a-million risk shouldn't outweigh a certain harm to thousands of students today," or "Even a small chance of an irreversible disaster deserves more weight than a modest, fixable cost." Good judges listen for which side explains its measure better.

example.title: Resolution: The United States should expand nuclear power. Final focus, both sides.

lines.s: Two impacts are left: their risk of an accident and our reduction in air pollution from fossil fuels. Weigh probability: air pollution from burning fossil fuels harms health every day, while serious nuclear accidents are rare. Weigh magnitude: pollution affects millions of people, not one region. So even if they're right that accidents are possible, our impact is certain and larger.

Weigh reversibility and timeframe. New reactors take many years to build, so their benefit is slow to arrive, while wind, solar and efficiency can cut emissions sooner. And a major accident can make an area unusable for a long time, which can't be quickly undone. When one option is slower and carries an irreversible risk, the judge should prefer the faster, safer path.

example.note: Both sides weighed using different measures and explained why their measure should count most. That gives the judge a clear choice.

list: "Even if they win ___, we still win because ___."
"Their impact depends on ours: if ___, then their harm never happens." (This is called **short-circuiting** or **pre-requisite** weighing.)
"This is the bigger issue because it affects more people for longer."

practice: Take two impacts from opposite sides of a topic page and write one weighing sentence for each of the four measures.
Write a 30-second "even if" statement that weighs your impact against the other side's strongest one.
Use the weighing practice in the drills.
